stem: A research agent runs 40-step investigations. Around step 25 it starts answering from details settled early in the run and stops honoring a rule set in the first turn, although the window is only half full. The team proposes moving to a model variant with a much larger context window. Which statement best evaluates that plan?

options.text: It will fix the problem if the team also raises max_tokens so the agent has enough room to reason through the accumulated material each turn.
options.why: max_tokens caps the output of one turn; it has no effect on stale material in the input competing with current instructions.

options.text: It will not fix the problem, because larger windows only work with prompt caching enabled.
options.why: Caching changes what tokens cost, not whether they occupy the window or how a larger window behaves. The reasoning is wrong even though the conclusion is right.

options.text: It will fix the problem, because the degradation is caused by the window running out of room and the rule being pushed out of the visible history.
options.why: The window is only half full, so capacity is not the constraint; the symptoms are attention-driven drift, not overflow.

options.text: It will not fix the problem, because spent context still competes for attention; prune or compact instead.
options.why: Context drift comes from finished work still occupying the window and diluting attention. A larger window preserves every distraction; curating what remains addresses the cause.

explanation: Bloat is a size problem; drift is an attention problem. When behavior degrades before the window is full, the fix is to change what the window holds (prune spent tool output, compact, isolate), not to add room that keeps every distraction at full weight.
reference: Claude API docs — Context windows; Anthropic engineering — Effective context engineering for AI agents

stem: A code-review agent's context grows mainly from `read_file` results that it can re-read at any time. The dialogue itself is short, and the agent must keep the exact wording of the reviewer's earlier decisions. Which context-management choice best fits?

options.text: Enable tool-result clearing so old file contents are removed while the turns stay intact.
options.why: Clearing removes old tool results and leaves a placeholder, but does not touch the dialogue, so exact decisions remain and any needed file can be re-read.

options.text: Move every file read into a subagent so the main agent never sees file contents and its own history stays flat.
options.why: A reviewer must read code directly; isolating every read adds latency and hides the evidence the agent's decisions rest on.

options.text: Enable compaction so the whole history, including the file contents and the reviewer's decisions, is rewritten as a summary.
options.why: Compaction rewrites the dialogue too, so the reviewer's exact decisions survive only if the summary keeps them. The bulk of the growth is re-fetchable tool output, which does not need summarizing.

options.text: Truncate the history to the last few turns whenever the request approaches the window limit.
options.why: Blind truncation discards the reviewer's decisions along with the file contents, with no summary and no placeholder.

explanation: Choose the lever by where the growth comes from. Re-fetchable tool output that is no longer needed is what tool-result clearing is for; compaction is for long dialogues where continuity matters and a summary is acceptable.
reference: Claude API docs — Context editing; Manage tool context

stem: In one Claude Code session a developer spent an hour debugging a payments bug, then asks Claude to design an unrelated onboarding flow. Suggestions keep referencing payments files, responses are slow, and each message costs more than expected. What should the developer do?

options.text: Switch to a larger context window so both tasks fit comfortably in one session.
options.why: Room is not the issue; irrelevant material still competes for attention and is still billed on every turn.

options.text: Run `/compact` so the payments work is summarized and stays available in case the new task needs it later.
options.why: Compaction keeps a summary of the payments work in context, which is exactly the material crowding out the unrelated task.

options.text: Run `/clear` to start the new task fresh, keeping durable notes in files or CLAUDE.md.
options.why: Unrelated work is the case for clearing: the old conversation costs tokens on every message and crowds out what the new task needs, and nothing from it is required.

options.text: Raise the auto-compact threshold so the session stops summarizing and keeps the whole payments conversation verbatim.
options.why: Keeping more of the payments conversation verbatim increases cost and distraction rather than reducing it.

explanation: Compaction preserves continuity for the same task; clearing is for switching to unrelated work, where old conversation only adds cost and noise. Anything worth keeping belongs in files, memory, or CLAUDE.md, not in the transcript.
reference: Claude Code docs — Explore the context window

stem: In a Claude Code session a developer explored a payments module, settled three design decisions with Claude in conversation, and also chased an unrelated logging issue that is now resolved. The context is about 70% full, and she is about to start a long implementation phase that depends on those decisions, which exist only in the transcript. What should she do before starting?

options.text: Run `/compact` with instructions naming the design decisions and payments files to keep.
options.why: A focused compaction keeps what the developer chooses, so the decisions survive and the resolved logging detour is dropped, instead of the automatic pass guessing what matters.

options.text: Run `/clear` so the implementation starts with an empty window and full room to work.
options.why: Clearing discards the decisions along with the noise; nothing was written to a file, so the next phase would have to rediscover them.

options.text: Keep working and let auto-compact run when the window fills, since it preserves the important parts automatically.
options.why: Auto-compact summarizes on its own judgment mid-phase, with no way to say which decisions matter, and the logging detour may be kept while a decision is dropped.

options.text: Raise the auto-compact threshold so the whole exploration stays verbatim through the implementation phase.
options.why: Keeping the resolved detour verbatim adds cost and distraction on every message and only postpones the summary to a worse moment.

explanation: Compaction is the lever for continuing the same task with less noise, and it can be steered: `/compact` with focus instructions before a long new phase keeps what you name rather than what the automatic pass guesses. Clearing is for unrelated work; waiting for auto-compact gives up control of timing and content.
reference: Claude Code docs — Explore the context window; Manage costs effectively

stem: A team using server-side compaction saw summaries drop order IDs, so they set custom compaction `instructions` to "Preserve all order IDs and error messages." Custom instructions replace the default summarization prompt entirely. Order IDs now survive, but after each compaction the agent forgets which steps it completed and which decisions were made. What should the developer do?

options.text: Expand the instructions so the summary also covers progress made, decisions with reasons, and open items.
options.why: Because the custom prompt is the whole summarization prompt, it must ask for everything a later turn needs, not just the identifiers that motivated the change.

options.text: Keep the one-line instructions and lower the compaction trigger so summaries are written more often during a task.
options.why: More frequent summaries written from the same narrow prompt still omit progress and decisions; frequency does not change content.

options.text: Keep the one-line instructions and list every order ID in the system prompt so the summary can stay short.
options.why: This addresses IDs, which already survive, and leaves the missing progress and decisions unaddressed.

options.text: Have the agent restate its completed steps in every reply so the summarizer sees them more often.
options.why: Restatements are input to a summarizer that was told to keep only IDs and errors; they are dropped like everything else not requested.

explanation: Custom compaction instructions are the summarization prompt, not an addition to it. A custom prompt must therefore cover everything a later turn needs: progress, decisions and their reasons, open items, and the exact identifiers that prompted the change.
reference: Claude API docs — Compaction at a token threshold; Compaction on demand

stem: To keep the main context small, a developer has Claude Code delegate everything to subagents: planning a feature, implementing it, and testing it each go to a separate subagent, and so does scanning a 20,000-line log for the failing request. Sessions became slower, the implementation subagent contradicts the plan, and the developer has to re-explain decisions at every step. Which split fits best?

options.text: Keep planning, implementation, and testing in the main conversation, and delegate only the log scan to a subagent.
options.why: Phases that share significant context and need back-and-forth belong in the main conversation; a subagent fits self-contained work with verbose output that should return as a summary, such as the log scan.

options.text: Keep the delegation but give each subagent every tool the main conversation has so it can rediscover the plan itself.
options.why: Rediscovery is the cost being paid; more tools make each fresh-context subagent slower and still leave the plan out of its context.

options.text: Run everything, including the log scan, in the main conversation so no context is ever lost between steps.
options.why: The log output would flood the main context; that is exactly the verbose, self-contained work isolation is for.

options.text: Replace the subagents with `/compact` between phases so each phase starts from a summary of the previous one.
options.why: The phases are not suffering from a full window; compacting between them adds lossy summaries where the phases need shared, verbatim context.

explanation: Context isolation is a tool, not a default. Use the main conversation when phases share significant context or need iterative back-and-forth; use a subagent when the work is self-contained and produces verbose output that only needs to come back as a summary. A non-fork subagent starts fresh, so every delegation pays a re-gathering cost.
reference: Claude Code docs — Create custom subagents

stem: A coding agent uses the memory tool across many sessions. Its memory directory now holds sixty ad-hoc files with overlapping notes, several stale, and each session spends its first dozen turns reading them before doing any work. Which two changes best fix this? (Choose two.)

options.text: Disable memory and rely on compaction summaries to carry state between sessions.
options.why: Compaction works within a conversation; it does not persist anything to a new session, and it is lossy by design.

options.text: Instruct the agent to keep memory coherent, merging or deleting files that are no longer relevant, and expire files unused for a long time.
options.why: The memory guidance recommends reinforcing organization and periodically deleting stale files so memory stays small and current.

options.text: Have the application load every memory file into the system prompt so no `view` calls are needed.
options.why: This moves the same bloat into every request and defeats the purpose of keeping knowledge outside the window.

options.text: Raise the context window so reading all sixty files at start is affordable.
options.why: Reading everything remains slow and dilutes attention; the fix is fewer, better files, not more room.

options.text: Set up a deliberate structure: one progress log and one feature checklist that each session reads at start and updates at end.
options.why: The documented multisession pattern uses a small set of known files as a recovery mechanism, so a session restores state without exploring a directory.

explanation: Memory is a recovery mechanism, not a dumping ground. A small, deliberate set of files (progress log, checklist, setup reference) that sessions read first and update last, plus instructions and housekeeping that keep memory coherent, is what makes multi-session work resume cleanly.
reference: Claude API docs — Memory tool

stem: A 60-page vendor contract is reviewed by an agent in isolated passes, one section per call with only that section in context. Local errors are caught reliably, but a clause in section 3 that contradicts a payment term in section 11 is missed every time. The team proposes running the whole contract through three full passes and taking a majority vote. Which approach is better?

options.text: Adopt the three-pass majority vote, since agreement across independent full passes is the standard way to make a review reliable.
options.why: Three passes over a whole contract repeat the same attention problem three times at triple cost; agreement on something all passes missed is not detection.

options.text: Keep the per-section passes, then add a comparison pass over the key terms extracted from every section.
options.why: A cross-section contradiction is visible only to a step whose scope includes both sections. Extracting terms first keeps that pass small and focused.

options.text: Merge everything into one call with the full contract and instruct the model to be extremely thorough about cross-references between sections.
options.why: A single long pass reintroduces the attention dilution that the section passes were designed to avoid, and thoroughness instructions do not change scope.

options.text: Raise the section size so each pass covers two adjacent sections at a time.
options.why: Sections 3 and 11 are not adjacent; overlapping windows still miss long-range contradictions.

explanation: Isolation is a scoping decision: each step should hold exactly the material its job needs. Local checks need local scope; contradictions need a step whose scope is the comparison itself, fed by condensed output from earlier steps rather than the raw document.
reference: Anthropic engineering — Effective context engineering for AI agents; Claude API docs — Prompting best practices

stem: In a procurement assistant, a user says in turn 3: "For this case, never contact Vendor Alpha." The conversation runs for hours with compaction triggering several times. After the third compaction the agent emails Vendor Alpha. The rule is specific to this conversation, not a standing policy, and the team must guarantee it holds no matter what future summaries keep. What should the developer do?

options.text: Have the agent restate the constraint in its own reply every few turns so it is always recent when the next summary is written.
options.why: Restatements sit in the region that compaction rewrites, so they are subject to the same loss.

options.text: Capture such constraints in per-conversation state that the application injects outside the compacted history every request.
options.why: Only content outside the compactable region is immune to what summaries omit. Injecting the constraint each turn, for example into that conversation's system prompt, makes it hold regardless of compaction.

options.text: Raise the compaction trigger so summaries happen less often during a case and the rule is rewritten fewer times.
options.why: This changes how often the loss can occur, not whether a summary may drop the rule.

options.text: Add "preserve all user-stated constraints exactly, including who must not be contacted" to the custom compaction instructions so every summary carries it forward.
options.why: This improves the odds but keeps the rule inside the lossy process; a summary of a summary can still drop it, so there is no guarantee.

explanation: A constraint that must hold for the whole run belongs outside what compaction may rewrite. Standing rules live in the system prompt; per-conversation constraints belong in application state that is reinjected each turn. Better summarization instructions and threshold tuning only change the odds and frequency of loss.
reference: Claude API docs — Compaction at a token threshold; Prompting best practices

stem:
An agent with 80 tools shows this usage on the first turn of a fresh conversation, before any tool result exists:
```
turn 1: input_tokens=62000, messages=1 (short user question)
turn 6: input_tokens=71000
```
Tool-result clearing is already enabled. Latency and cost per turn are dominated by the baseline, and only a few tools are used in any conversation. What should the developer do first?

options.text: Lower the tool-result clearing trigger so results are pruned sooner and the growth between turn 1 and turn 6 is contained.
options.why: Turn 1 has no tool results at all, so the 62k baseline cannot come from them; clearing cannot reduce it.

options.text: Enable compaction so the conversation is summarized before it grows, bringing the per-turn input back toward the baseline.
options.why: Compaction rewrites conversation turns; the cost here is a fixed 60k prefix present before any turn accumulates.

options.text: Load tool definitions on demand with tool search so only the tools a conversation needs enter the context.
options.why: The baseline is tool definitions sent every request. Deferring them until Claude asks trades one lookup turn for a large reduction in baseline context.

options.text: Move the tool definitions into the system prompt with a cache breakpoint so they are counted once and read from cache thereafter.
options.why: Definitions occupy the window wherever they sit; relocating them changes nothing about their size.

explanation: Diagnose which source of context pressure you have. Tool definitions sit at the front of every request and answer to neither clearing nor compaction; the documented answer for large, mostly unused toolsets is to defer definitions until requested. Caching would reduce cost but not the tokens in context.
reference: Claude API docs — Manage tool context

stem: A developer iterates on a flaky integration suite in one Claude Code session. Each run prints thousands of lines of passing-test output, and Claude then reads a 10,000-line service log to find the failing request. After a few iterations most of the context is test and log output, responses slow down, and Claude starts missing details from earlier in the same task. The developer needs the iteration to continue in this session. Which two changes best fix this? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add a hook that filters the test command's output so only failures reach Claude.
options.why: A hook can preprocess output before Claude sees it, turning thousands of lines into the handful that matter, so the noise never enters the context.

options.text: Run `/clear` after every test run and describe the failure again from scratch.
options.why: Clearing throws away the task in progress; the developer needs continuity across iterations.

options.text: Delegate the log search to a subagent that returns only the failing request and its stack trace.
options.why: Verbose reads belong in a subagent's context; only the summary comes back, so the main conversation keeps its earlier details.

options.text: Raise the auto-compact threshold so more of the test output stays verbatim between iterations.
options.why: Keeping more raw output in the window increases the bloat that is causing the slowdown and missed details.

options.text: Paste the full log into CLAUDE.md so it loads once at startup instead of on every read.
options.why: CLAUDE.md content enters every session's context; this moves the bloat to the front of every conversation.

explanation: Context bloat from tool output is best handled at the source: filter output before Claude sees it, and send high-volume reads to a subagent so only a summary returns. Clearing sacrifices continuity, and keeping more raw output only deepens the bloat.
reference: Claude Code docs — Manage costs effectively; Explore the context window

stem: A long-running agent must see an up-to-date task board (open items, remaining budget) on every turn. The harness currently edits the previous user message to swap in the new board each turn. Cache reads have fallen to near zero, and some requests are now rejected with a 400 because earlier thinking blocks no longer match the prefix they were generated against. Which change satisfies freshness, cache economy, and correctness?

options.text: Send the board once at the start of the conversation and rely on compaction summaries to keep the open items and budget current.
options.why: The board changes every turn; a summary of an old board is stale, and compaction runs only occasionally.

options.text: Strip all thinking blocks from history before each request so prefix mismatches cannot occur, and keep editing the board in place.
options.why: Removing thinking blocks is itself a history edit that discards reasoning continuity; it also does nothing for the cache misses caused by rewriting earlier turns.

options.text: Put the task board in the top-level system prompt and regenerate it every turn so it always carries system authority and current values.
options.why: A changing system prompt alters the very start of the prefix, so the cache restarts every turn; freshness is met but cost is not.

options.text: Keep the history append-only and add the board at the end of each request, as a mid-conversation system message where supported.
options.why: Appending leaves the cached prefix and earlier thinking blocks untouched, while the board still arrives with system authority and current values.

explanation: Rewriting earlier turns restarts the prompt cache and can invalidate preserved thinking. Dynamic per-turn context should be appended, not spliced into history: the prefix stays byte-identical, and a mid-conversation system message carries the same authority as the system field without invalidating what came before it.
reference: Claude API docs — Mid-conversation system messages and tool changes; Using the Messages API

stem: A prompt that extracts line items from receipts handles printed receipts well but fails on handwritten totals and receipts with a tip added after the total. A developer adds twenty more examples, all of clean printed receipts. Accuracy on the failing cases does not move and cost per request rises. What should the developer do instead?

options.text: Remove all examples and describe the extraction rules for handwritten totals and tips in more detail instead.
options.why: Descriptions leave margins to inference; a worked instance of the awkward case settles them more reliably than more prose.

options.text: Keep the examples and raise the temperature so the model explores other layouts rather than copying the printed pattern.
options.why: Sampling settings do not teach the model how to handle a layout it was never shown.

options.text: Add twenty further printed examples so the pattern is reinforced more strongly and the model generalizes it to handwritten cases.
options.why: More examples of the case that already works optimizes the distribution that was never failing.

options.text: Replace the set with a few diverse examples drawn from the failing cases, such as handwritten totals and added tips.
options.why: Examples steer format and edge handling best when they are relevant, diverse, and few (roughly three to five); they must come from the population that fails.

explanation: Few-shot examples work when they mirror the real task, vary enough to cover edge cases, and are kept to a handful. Volume of clean examples adds cost without covering the cases that fail.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompting best practices

stem: A prompt for triaging bug reports says: "Be precise and thorough, and assign an appropriate severity." Reviewers disagree about whether outputs are acceptable, and severity labels vary between runs on identical reports. Applying the "show it to a colleague with minimal context" test, what is the most effective revision?

options.text: Name the allowed severity values with a rule for each, and state the required length and fields of the output.
options.why: An instruction is checkable when output can be tested against it: a fixed set of values, defined criteria, and a stated shape.

options.text: Give the model a role such as "senior support engineer with ten years of triage experience" and leave the rest unchanged.
options.why: A role focuses tone and framing but does not supply the missing definitions that make outputs gradeable.

options.text: Add "It is critical that you are precise and thorough" in capitals at the top of the prompt so the instruction is not overlooked.
options.why: Restating a vague instruction more forcefully names no criterion and gives the model nothing new to comply with.

options.text: Set the temperature to zero so identical reports produce identical severity labels on every run.
options.why: Lower temperature reduces variation but does not define what severity means or which label is right.

explanation: Clear, direct instructions are ones a person with no context could follow and be judged against. Replace moods like "precise" with named permitted values, decision rules, and an explicit output shape.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompting best practices

stem: A team's Claude Code setup keeps everything in the project CLAUDE.md: build commands, a 60-step release procedure, and a paragraph explaining when the `run_migration` tool must not be used. Sessions start with a large context, the release steps are followed inconsistently, and the agent still runs migrations at the wrong time. Which two placements fix this? (Choose two.)

options.text: Move the build commands into a path-scoped rule so they load only when build files are read.
options.why: Build commands are needed in every session; scoping them to paths means they are absent when needed.

options.text: Split the CLAUDE.md into several imported files so each is under the size guidance.
options.why: Imported files still load at launch and enter context, so the total stays the same.

options.text: Move the release procedure into a skill so it loads only when a release is being done.
options.why: Multi-step procedures belong in skills that load on demand; CLAUDE.md is for facts that must hold in every session.

options.text: Duplicate the migration rule in CLAUDE.md, the system prompt, and each user message so it cannot be missed.
options.why: Copies drift and inflate every request; repetition is not what makes a rule reach the decision point.

options.text: Put the when-to-use and when-not-to-use guidance in the `run_migration` tool description.
options.why: Guidance about a tool is read at the moment the model decides whether to call it when it lives in that tool's description.

explanation: Place each instruction by lifetime and moment of use: always-true facts in CLAUDE.md, on-demand procedures in skills, path-specific rules scoped by path, and tool-choice guidance in the tool description where the model reads it while choosing.
reference: Claude Code docs — How Claude remembers your project; Claude API docs — Define tools

stem: A contract-review feature sends each clause with the user message "Review this clause." The answers are accurate but generic: they read like a general explanation rather than the risk-focused assessment a corporate lawyer would give, and the tone varies between requests. Which change most directly addresses this?

options.text: Set a specific role in the system prompt, such as general counsel at a software company reviewing contracts.
options.why: A role in the system prompt focuses Claude's behavior and tone for the use case; even one sentence shifts a generic explanation toward the framing and priorities of that role.

options.text: Raise the effort setting so the model reasons longer before answering each clause and covers more angles.
options.why: More reasoning does not tell the model whose perspective and priorities the review should reflect; the answer stays generic.

options.text: Add "be more professional and thorough, as a lawyer would be" to each user message.
options.why: This names a mood, not a perspective; it does not define what a legal reviewer would look for.

options.text: Prefix each clause with three example reviews written in the desired tone and level of detail.
options.why: Examples steer format and edge handling, but a role is the direct, cheaper way to set perspective and tone, and three examples per request add cost to every call.

explanation: Setting a role in the system prompt is a documented way to focus Claude's behavior and tone for a use case. When output is correct but generic, the missing ingredient is usually perspective, which a specific role supplies more directly than mood words, extra reasoning, or per-request examples.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompting best practices

stem: An internal tool asks Claude to "Create an analytics dashboard" from a data description. The output is a minimal page with one table. The product team expected filters, charts, and drill-downs, and assumed a more capable model would add them. Which change most reliably produces the richer result?

options.text: State the wanted scope explicitly: filters, charts, drill-downs, and a fully featured implementation beyond the basics.
options.why: Claude does what is asked; ambitious behavior must be requested explicitly rather than inferred from a vague prompt.

options.text: Switch to the most capable model and keep the prompt unchanged, since stronger models add more on their own.
options.why: A stronger model still follows the instruction as given; the prompt asked for a dashboard, not an elaborate one.

options.text: Raise max_tokens so the model has room to produce a larger and more complete page.
options.why: The output limit was not reached; the model stopped because it had done what was asked.

options.text: Raise the temperature so the model explores more ambitious and varied designs.
options.why: Sampling settings affect randomness, not the scope of what the model decides to build.

explanation: Be clear and direct: Claude responds to explicit instructions and does not add unrequested scope on its own. When you want above-and-beyond behavior, name it in the prompt instead of relying on the model, its size, or sampling settings to infer it.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompting best practices

stem: A summarization prompt passes every accuracy eval, but the product's p95 latency target is missed. The team has spent two weeks trimming words from the prompt and rephrasing instructions with no measurable change. What should they do next?

options.text: Add few-shot examples of short summaries so the model produces fewer output tokens and finishes sooner.
options.why: Examples steer format; if output length were the bottleneck, an explicit length constraint would already have shown an effect.

options.text: Relax the latency target since accuracy is already met and further prompt work is unlikely to move it.
options.why: Changing the success criterion to fit the result is not a solution when a legitimate lever exists.

options.text: Continue shortening the prompt and removing examples until the latency target is met, re-running accuracy evals each time.
options.why: Two weeks of prompt edits produced no change, which is evidence that latency is not controlled by this prompt's wording.

options.text: Treat this as a model and configuration decision, evaluating a faster model or effort setting on the same evals.
options.why: Not every failing criterion is a prompting problem; latency and cost are the documented examples that a different model choice often settles more easily.

explanation: Prompt engineering is scoped to criteria that wording can control. When evals show quality is fine and the failing criterion is latency or cost, the right move is usually model selection or configuration, validated against the same test set.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompt engineering overview

stem: A pipeline inserts Claude's summary directly into a document. Responses often begin with "Here is the summary:" and end with "Let me know if you need changes." The developer runs a current model, so prefilling the assistant turn is not available. Which approach most reliably yields only the summary text?

options.text: Delete the first and last sentence of every response in post-processing, since that is where the extra lines appear.
options.why: This destroys real content whenever the model does not add a preamble or closing line.

options.text: Instruct the model to answer without preamble and put the summary inside a named tag, then extract that tag in code.
options.why: Direct format instructions plus a tag as the format indicator give a stable stopping point and something code can extract; stray text outside the tag is harmless.

options.text: Lower max_tokens so there is no room for a closing sentence after the summary has been written.
options.why: A token cap truncates the summary itself before it removes a trailing line.

options.text: Add an assistant message containing "Summary:" at the end of the request so the response continues from it.
options.why: That is a prefill on the final assistant turn, which current models reject with a 400 error.

explanation: Output constraints name a form and a stopping point. Without prefill, the documented migrations are direct instructions (no preamble), XML format indicators, structured outputs, or tool calling, with light post-processing only for the rare slip.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompting best practices

stem: A due-diligence assistant answers questions over three 30k-token filings placed at the top of the prompt in `<document>` tags with `<source>` metadata, and the question at the end. Answers are mostly right but sometimes blend facts from the wrong filing or cite nothing. Which two changes best improve grounding without changing the architecture? (Choose two.)

options.text: Ask the model to first extract the relevant quotes from the documents into a tagged section, then answer using only those quotes.
options.why: Quote-first grounding focuses attention on the relevant passages and makes the answer traceable to exact text.

options.text: Move the question and instructions above the documents so they are read first.
options.why: Long documents belong at the top; queries at the end improve quality, so this reverses a documented best practice.

options.text: Require each claim in the answer to reference the document index or source it came from.
options.why: Per-claim attribution forces the model to tie each fact to a specific filing, exposing cross-document blending.

options.text: Concatenate the three filings into one untagged block to reduce token overhead from tags.
options.why: Removing document boundaries makes blending more likely and destroys the metadata attribution needs.

options.text: Raise the temperature so the model considers more of the text.
options.why: Sampling settings do not affect which passages the model attends to or whether it cites them.

explanation: For long-document prompts, keep documents at the top with clear per-document structure, put the query last, and have the model quote relevant passages before answering. Requiring per-claim attribution makes grounding checkable and reveals cross-document confusion.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompting best practices; Reduce hallucinations

stem: A ticket classifier has category definitions in its system prompt and returns labels via an enum. Its eval scores 91% overall, but 35% of true `refund_request` tickets are labeled `billing_question`, and the reverse error is rare. Adding eight more `billing_question` examples last sprint did not change this. Which single change is most likely to fix the failing category?

options.text: Remove the `billing_question` category so refund tickets have nowhere else to go, and handle billing questions with a keyword filter.
options.why: Real billing questions still arrive; deleting the category trades one error class for a larger one.

options.text: Add more `billing_question` examples so the model sees the common category often enough to learn its full range.
options.why: This was already tried and cannot help: the failing population is refund tickets, and the boundary between the two categories is what is undefined.

options.text: Switch to a more capable model and keep the prompt unchanged, since the boundary is a matter of judgment.
options.why: A stronger model may lower the error rate but the boundary is unspecified; the class of failure remains.

options.text: Add a decision rule plus contrasting example pairs (a refund request beside a similar billing question) taken from the misclassified tickets.
options.why: Category boundaries drift when a definition leaves edges open; a rule plus contrastive examples from the failing cases closes exactly the edge that fails.

explanation: Iterate from the eval failure, not the aggregate score. A one-directional confusion between two categories is a boundary problem: state the rule that separates them and demonstrate it with contrasting pairs taken from the tickets that failed.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompting best practices; Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem: An invoice extractor returned an empty `po_number` field for about 10% of invoices, where the number sat in a footer or a cover note rather than the header. A developer made the field required and non-null in the schema; empties disappeared, but a later audit finds invented PO numbers on exactly those invoices. Which single change best fixes the root cause?

options.text: Keep the field required and add "never guess a PO number; search the whole document carefully" to the instructions.
options.why: The schema still forbids the honest answer; a prohibition supplies no method for finding the value, so guessing continues.

options.text: Add examples showing extraction from footers and cover notes, and allow null with a reason when none is present.
options.why: Examples move attention to where the value actually sits, and permitting an explicit absent case removes the pressure to invent.

options.text: Retry any response whose `po_number` matches a known invented pattern until a different value appears in the output.
options.why: Retrying until something looks plausible is a search whose verdict is fixed in advance; it produces different inventions.

options.text: Raise the model's thinking effort so it searches the document more carefully before filling in the required field.
options.why: More reasoning about a schema that forbids "not found" still yields a fabricated number when the value is missing.

explanation: A constraint on form cannot generate content that was never found. Marking a field non-nullable turns an absent value into an invented one. Fix the search with examples from the failing locations and give the model an honest way to report absence.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompting best practices; Reduce hallucinations

stem: A policy assistant answers from retrieved documents. Its system prompt says: "Always provide a definitive answer. Never say you do not know." Evals show that when retrieval returns no relevant document, the assistant states policy numbers and effective dates that do not exist, and reviewers cannot tell these from grounded answers. Which single prompt change is most effective?

options.text: Add "double-check every fact against the retrieved documents before answering" to the system prompt.
options.why: There is nothing to check against when retrieval is empty; the instruction still demands an answer.

options.text: Ask the model to add a confidence score to each answer and hide answers scored below a threshold.
options.why: Self-reported confidence comes from the same generation as the answer and is highest on the confidently wrong cases.

options.text: Lower the temperature so fabricated numbers are at least consistent between runs and easier to spot.
options.why: Consistency of a fabrication does not make it true or detectable.

options.text: Replace the rule with: answer only from the supplied documents, and say "I don't have enough information" when they do not cover the question.
options.why: Restricting to provided sources and explicitly permitting uncertainty are the documented levers that remove the incentive to invent.

explanation: An instruction that forbids "I don't know" forces fabrication whenever the sources are silent. Allow uncertainty explicitly and restrict answers to the provided documents; then unanswerable cases become visible and routable instead of confidently wrong.
reference: Claude API docs — Reduce hallucinations

stem: A team is deciding where each piece of guidance for a Messages API research agent should live. The agent has standing operator rules, a `search_docs` tool that must not be called for questions about pricing, retrieved articles that arrive through that tool, and a rule that appears mid-session ("from now on, cite only sources dated this year") after many cached turns. Which three placements are correct? (Choose three.)

options.text: Standing operator rules in the top-level system prompt.
options.why: Rules you wrote that apply to the whole conversation belong in the system field, where they carry operator authority and stay in the cached prefix.

options.text: The pricing restriction in the `search_docs` tool description.
options.why: Guidance about when not to use a tool is read at the moment Claude decides whether to call it when it lives in that tool's description.

options.text: Retrieved articles inside the tool result, JSON-encoded, with the system prompt stating that tool content is data.
options.why: Third-party content belongs only in tool results, where Claude treats embedded instructions with skepticism; the policy that it is data belongs in the system prompt.

options.text: The mid-session citation rule added to the top-level system prompt when it arises.
options.why: Editing the system field changes the start of the prefix and invalidates the cache for every turn after it; append the rule as a mid-conversation system message instead.

options.text: Retrieved articles pasted into the system prompt so they are read with full authority.
options.why: Content in the system prompt carries the authority of your rules, so an instruction hidden in an article would be followed as policy.

options.text: The pricing restriction appended to the end of each tool result returned by `search_docs`.
options.why: Your own instructions inside a tool result sit in the untrusted channel and may be discounted or flagged as injection.

explanation: Place each instruction by who wrote it and when it must be read: standing operator rules in the system prompt, tool-use guidance in the tool description, third-party content only in tool results with the data policy stated in the system prompt, and later-arriving rules appended as mid-conversation system messages rather than edits to the cached prefix.
reference: Claude API docs — Prompting best practices; Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections; Mid-conversation system messages and tool changes

stem: A router uses structured outputs with an enum of topics such as `"account access"` and `"billing dispute"`. The response completes normally, but a `switch` statement occasionally falls through to its default branch because the value arrived as `"Billing Dispute"`. What should the developer do?

options.text: Check `stop_reason` for a special value that indicates an enum mismatch.
options.why: No error and no special stop reason is returned for this case; the response looks complete.

options.text: Treat the response as a schema violation and retry the request until the exact lowercase string appears.
options.why: Capitalization of enum values is not guaranteed, so retries waste calls on a documented, harmless variation.

options.text: Compare enum values case-insensitively in code, and avoid enum members that differ only by case.
options.why: This is the documented handling: structured outputs guarantee the enum's words, not their capitalization.

options.text: Add `strict: true` to the schema so capitalization is enforced by the compiled grammar rather than by code.
options.why: The capitalization caveat applies to both JSON outputs and strict tool use; strictness does not change it.

explanation: Structured outputs constrain shape, but enum and const values may come back with different capitalization and no signal. Defensive parsing normalizes case on receipt, and the schema should never rely on case to distinguish values.
reference: Claude API docs — Structured outputs

stem: A developer writes a JSON schema with `"age": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 0, "maximum": 150}`, passes it through the SDK's structured-output helper (which strips unsupported keywords such as `minimum`/`maximum` before sending), and parses responses with a plain JSON parser. A response arrives with `age: 900` and the pipeline writes it to the database. The developer believed structured outputs guaranteed the range. What is the correct understanding and fix?

options.text: The range was honored but the model misread the document; add a retry with a stronger model for out-of-range values.
options.why: The value violates the declared range, so the constraint was not enforced at generation time; a model swap does not add enforcement.

options.text: Range keywords are not enforced at generation time, so application code must validate ranges on receipt and route failures.
options.why: Structured outputs guarantee structure and types; range and length keywords such as `minimum` and `maximum` are not part of the grammar (SDK helpers strip them and validate afterwards), so the application must enforce them on the response.

options.text: Ranges are enforced only when `additionalProperties` is set to false on the object; add that to the model definition.
options.why: `additionalProperties: false` controls extra keys, not numeric ranges.

options.text: Structured outputs enforce ranges only for tool inputs, so move the extraction into a tool with `strict: true`.
options.why: The same transformation applies to strict tool schemas; ranges are validated by the application either way.

explanation: Structured outputs guarantee structure and types, not every JSON Schema keyword. Range and length constraints are not enforced at generation; SDK helpers strip them from the wire schema and validate the response themselves, and code that parses raw responses must do the same. Validate on receipt and give failures a destination.
reference: Claude API docs — Structured outputs

stem: A moderation pipeline uses structured outputs. For some inputs the JSON parser throws, and logs show the response was HTTP 200 with `stop_reason: "refusal"`. The team's fix is to catch the parse error and resend the identical request up to five times before giving up. What is the better handling?

options.text: Wrap the schema in a tool with `strict: true` so a refusal is forced into the schema and the parser never sees free text.
options.why: Schema compliance is not guaranteed on a refusal; the refusal takes precedence over the grammar regardless of mechanism.

options.text: Check `stop_reason` before parsing, and route refusals to a separate path such as a fallback model or review.
options.why: Refusals arrive as normal 200 responses; branching on `stop_reason` first avoids the parser and lets the application handle the case deliberately, including a fallback model where appropriate.

options.text: Return an empty moderation result for refused items so the pipeline never blocks on them.
options.why: Silently treating a refused item as clean removes the failure from view rather than from the system.

options.text: Keep the retries but add exponential backoff, since refusals are transient like rate limits and usually clear on a later attempt.
options.why: A refusal is a classifier decision on the content, not a transient failure; resending the same request repeats the same outcome.

explanation: A refusal is a distinct stop reason, not an error and not a transient fault. Defensive output handling reads `stop_reason` before content, treats refusal as its own branch, and gives it a destination such as a fallback model or a review queue.
reference: Claude API docs — Stop reasons and fallback; Structured outputs

stem: An extraction job returns a large JSON array. About 2% of responses end mid-object with `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`. An engineer proposes a repair function that closes any open brackets and braces so the partial array can be saved. What should the team do instead?

options.text: Detect `max_tokens` before parsing and retry with a higher limit, or split the input so each response fits.
options.why: Truncation is a signal to retry with enough room; structure cut mid-object should never be salvaged as if it were complete.

options.text: Ask the model to return fewer fields per item so the array is shorter and fits within the current limit.
options.why: Dropping fields sacrifices needed data to avoid handling a documented stop reason correctly.

options.text: Treat `max_tokens` responses as refusals and send them to human review with the partial output attached.
options.why: Truncation is not a refusal; it has a direct automated remedy, and review queues should hold real judgment cases.

options.text: Adopt the repair function, since most of the array is intact and the missing tail can be filled in by a later job.
options.why: A repaired fragment silently drops trailing records and may corrupt the last one; the pipeline reports success on incomplete data.

explanation: Schema compliance is not guaranteed when the output limit is hit. Branch on `stop_reason: max_tokens`, then retry with a higher limit or reduce the work per request. Salvaging fragments hides data loss behind a successful-looking run.
reference: Claude API docs — Structured outputs; Stop reasons and fallback

stem: A consumer service parses JSON produced by an upstream Claude step. Last month it crashed when a new `notes` field appeared; the hotfix now silently discards any record that fails validation, and a numeric `quantity` that arrives as the string "n/a" is coerced to 0. Which two changes make the parsing defensive without hiding problems? (Choose two.)

options.text: Coerce every unparsable number to 0 so downstream arithmetic never fails.
options.why: A failed conversion turned into zero invents a value; a string that is not a number is a rejection, not a quantity.

options.text: Reject records with type mismatches or missing required values into a queue with a log line and metric.
options.why: Rejections that are visible and counted give the failure a destination and make the rate observable.

options.text: Fail the entire batch whenever any single record does not validate.
options.why: Crashing on anything unfamiliar is the outage the team was asked to prevent.

options.text: Ignore unknown fields but log their arrival, since a new field signals a producer change.
options.why: Tolerating extras keeps the service running while surfacing the change to someone who can act on it.

options.text: Keep discarding invalid records so the pipeline always reports success.
options.why: The silent drop is the worse failure: records vanish and the success metric lies.

explanation: Defensive parsing survives surprises and still reports them: tolerate unknown fields, keep absent, null, and empty distinct, reject rather than coerce a guess, and route every rejection somewhere visible. Neither crashing nor silently dropping is acceptable.
reference: Claude API docs — Structured outputs; Stop reasons and fallback

stem: An Agent SDK application requests a JSON schema output format. The code treats any result whose `subtype` is `success` as complete and reads `result.structured_output`. Downstream jobs occasionally receive `null` and crash. What should the developer change?

options.text: Parse the agent's final text message as JSON whenever `structured_output` is missing, since it usually contains the answer.
options.why: The final text is not validated against the schema; falling back to it reintroduces the malformed-output problem the schema was meant to solve.

options.text: Remove the schema and validate the text output in the application instead, so there is only one code path.
options.why: This discards the SDK's validation and re-prompting and gives up the guarantee for no gain.

options.text: Raise the maximum turns so the agent always has enough time to produce the structured output before the run ends.
options.why: More turns may help some runs but does not fix code that accepts a success result with no structured output.

options.text: Accept a result only when `subtype` is `success` and `structured_output` is present; treat every other case as a failure.
options.why: A run can finish with `success` and no structured output; that case must be treated as a failure alongside `error_max_structured_output_retries`.

explanation: With Agent SDK structured outputs, success of the run and presence of validated output are separate facts. Check both, and treat a missing `structured_output` or a retry-exhausted error as failures with their own handling.
reference: Agent SDK docs — Get structured output from agents

stem: A pipeline extracts revenue, cost, and margin from quarterly filings with structured outputs. Every response is schema-valid and confidently worded, yet reconciliation found several wrong margins. Re-running the same filing produces the same wrong figure each time. The team can afford some extra code but not a doubling of model calls. Which two safeguards would catch these errors? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add a `confidence` field to the schema and reject extractions below 0.8.
options.why: Self-reported confidence is produced by the same generation as the figure and is highest exactly where the answer is confidently wrong.

options.text: Recompute margin from the extracted revenue and cost in code and flag any mismatch with the reported margin.
options.why: Arithmetic is an independent authority the model did not produce; a derived value that fails to reconcile is caught deterministically at no model cost.

options.text: Run each extraction three times and accept the majority value automatically.
options.why: The errors are stable across runs, so a vote converges on the same wrong figure, and it triples model calls.

options.text: Require the exact source text for each figure and verify in code that it appears in the filing, routing misses to a reviewer.
options.why: Checking the quoted passage against the document is a verification whose truth comes from outside the model.

options.text: Tighten the schema so margin must be a number between 0 and 100.
options.why: A plausible wrong margin still passes a range check; this answers the shape question, not the truth question.

explanation: Schema-valid is not correct. A check catches a confident wrong answer only if its truth comes from outside the model: recompute derived values, verify quoted sources against the document, and route violations to a person. Confidence scores and majority votes are correlated with the error they are meant to catch.
reference: Claude API docs — Reduce hallucinations; Structured outputs

stem: A benefits assistant retrieves two internal documents that state different effective dates for the same policy change, one from HR and one from Legal. Today it reports one date with full confidence, and case workers act on it. Which output-handling design best fits the fact that a person will make a decision from this answer?

options.text: Have the model keep searching until a third document confirms one of the dates, then report the confirmed one.
options.why: Searching until something backs one candidate is a hunt whose verdict is fixed in advance and may still land on the wrong date.

options.text: Ask the model to reason step by step about which source is more authoritative and commit to the date it finds most plausible.
options.why: Reasoning cannot manufacture the missing fact of which document is authoritative; it produces a confident single answer where the sources disagree.

options.text: Instruct the model to prefer the more recent document and report that date only, since policy changes supersede earlier ones.
options.why: Recency is a preference, not a finding; the older document may be the authoritative one, and the conflict is hidden from the decision maker.

options.text: Return both dates with their sources, mark the conflict, and route the case for confirmation when the date is decision-critical.
options.why: An answer that represents the disagreement with provenance is the accurate one; the person can resolve it with information the model lacks.

explanation: When credible sources disagree, a single confident answer is manufactured rather than found. Skepticism toward confident output means carrying the conflict and its provenance into the result and letting a human resolve what the model cannot.
reference: Claude API docs — Reduce hallucinations; Citations

stem: A SaaS product generates a distinct structured-output schema per customer by adding that customer's optional custom fields, many with nullable union types, to a shared base. Symptoms: the first request for each customer is noticeably slow, some customers get a 400 "schema is too complex for compilation", and latency worsens as customers add fields. Which change best resolves all three?

options.text: Split each customer's schema across several strict tools so that no single schema exceeds the compilation limits.
options.why: Complexity limits apply across all strict schemas in a request; splitting does not reduce the total and adds tool-selection risk.

options.text: Pre-warm every customer's schema at deploy time so the first request is fast, and re-warm whenever a customer adds a field.
options.why: Warming spreads the compilation cost but does not fix schemas that fail to compile or grow without bound.

options.text: Use one stable, simplified shared schema, carrying customer-specific fields as name-value entries inside it.
options.why: A single schema compiles once and stays cached; removing per-customer optional and union parameters removes the complexity that grows grammar size and causes the 400.

options.text: Drop structured outputs and ask for JSON in the prompt, validating against the customer's schema afterwards with retries.
options.why: This gives up guaranteed structure for every customer to fix a problem caused by schema design, and pushes format failures downstream.

explanation: Grammar compilation cost scales with optional and union parameters and is cached per schema. A stable, simple schema shared across tenants, with variability moved into values rather than structure, removes first-request latency, avoids the complexity limit, and keeps the guarantee.
reference: Claude API docs — Structured outputs

stem: A document classifier uses structured outputs with `category` as a required enum of six document types. Out-of-scope uploads such as photos and blank pages are always assigned one of the six, and downstream teams process them as if they were real. A single global confidence threshold was tried and rejected too many valid documents. Which single change best fixes this?

options.text: Add explicit outcomes to the schema, such as `out_of_scope` and `unreadable` with a reason, and route each differently.
options.why: A schema that names the honest outcomes lets the model report them and lets code branch on category rather than on a threshold.

options.text: Add a system prompt line saying "only classify real documents; skip photos and blank pages" and keep the six-value enum.
options.why: The enum still forces one of six values; an instruction cannot override a grammar that has no honest option.

options.text: Run the classifier twice and reject any upload where the two labels disagree, since out-of-scope inputs classify inconsistently.
options.why: A blank page can be labeled consistently both times; agreement is not evidence of scope, and calls double.

options.text: Lower the confidence threshold until valid documents stop being rejected, then filter out-of-scope uploads with a size check.
options.why: One number cannot separate an out-of-scope upload from a hard-to-read valid one; tuning it trades one error for the other.

explanation: A constrained output can only express the outcomes its schema allows. When inputs outside the intended set exist, give the schema named categories for them (absent-optional, unreadable, out of scope) and route on the category, rather than forcing a label and filtering by a single confidence cut.
reference: Claude API docs — Structured outputs; Reduce hallucinations
